i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. in the past, species from non-native regions have been introduced to the area in order to exploit and hunt them. consider the european rabbit that was smuggled to australia in the 18th century. this has become a real scourge of the land, as we know, because of the lack of natural enemies. the 300 million rabbits that are now living in the wild are responsible for destroying the flora of vast areas of land and are causing serious damage to agriculture. the fact that since the arrival of europeans in australia alone, 36 species have gone extinct and another 45 are endangered or threatened should serve as a warning example. but there are also examples from the native plant world. for example, if you walk through the countryside in my home country of carinthia today with your eyes open, you will notice the massive spread of the japanese perennial, which has escaped from the gardens as an ornamental plant. this is causing the displacement of parts of the native flora and consequently also of native animal species. it is therefore of the utmost importance to restrict not only the trade in wild fauna and flora but also the introduction of invasive species in order to protect native flora and fauna from competition, disease and displacement and ultimately extinction. i think we owe it to our children.

in writing. - this report on the european parliament's consent procedures points out a very important point in voting. the question arises as to whether, if the necessary majority is not reached and no amendment to the contrary is tabled, a decision is taken in the sense that the committee or the plenary did not take a decision, or in the sense of a decision to the contrary of what was proposed. the rapporteur, however, argues that it could be argued that consent must be given by a positive act and not by interpreting an act of parliament to the contrary. in order to avoid any difficulties, acts which do not reach the required majority should be considered as rejected. in this sense, the report is to be welcomed, since it encourages a clear decision and not the opposite interpretation in the absence of a positive vote.

in writing. the rapporteur draws attention to the recent food fraud incidents which have seriously damaged the confidence of european citizens. according to de lange, these cases of food fraud are far too rarely detected because there are no direct consequences for public health. it is further noted that food fraud occurs whenever the economic benefit is significantly higher than the sanctions and fines that would be expected if it were discovered. it is therefore required that the penalties be set at at least twice the amount of the economic advantage sought by the food fraud. the report can therefore be seen as very positive, since the shortcomings are known and steps are being taken and taken in the right direction.
in writing. − we must work together to tackle undeclared work in the eu. i therefore welcome the european parliament's own-initiative report, which aims to coordinate all national control authorities to combat illegal employment throughout europe. almost 20% of the eu's economic output comes from the black economy. this is not only a huge tax failure, but also a massive social problem and a distortion of competition in the eu. the epp delegation in the european parliament therefore today agrees with the european parliament's call for the establishment of a european coordination centre for all national labour inspectorates and competent control authorities to combat social dumping and illegal employment. the aim is not to centralize labour controls at eu level, but to strengthen national labour inspectorates and to commit them to cooperate. the aim is to establish an early warning system which will enable information to be exchanged between national authorities in the event of illegal practices by companies. the european parliament also wants joint training for their managers and the introduction of a european social security card that is counterfeit-proof. the increasing number of crossborder employment relationships means that labour inspectorates and financial supervisors must also cooperate across borders to combat undeclared work.
in writing. - black labour and the exploitation of workers are among the biggest problems facing european labour markets today, alongside unemployment. it is a fundamental task of the european union to ensure that mobile workers are protected in the internal market. we need effective labour inspectorates in europe to do this. i voted for the report by mrs jutta steinruck because it contains the following important points: (a) the supervisory powers of the public authorities must not be limited and must extend to all categories of workers. in writing. − i am pleased to see that the european parliament is advocating for greater involvement of employees in the success of companies. the aim is to ensure that employers share their profits with those who have made a significant contribution to them. this approach is mutually beneficial, as it motivates employees and thereby strengthens the competitiveness of companies. the basic condition for profit sharing is the economic success of the enterprise. if this is not available, then no surplus can be distributed. however, if a company makes a profit, each employee receives a share of it in addition to his regular salary. it is also important that all workers are equally integrated into this system in order to avoid injustices and ensure a fair distribution.
in writing. − employee financial participation is a very useful way for some companies to improve the stability and sustainability of the business. as a shadow rapporteur, i have been able to make many important points in this report and i therefore vote in favour. however, models of employee financial participation are not suitable for all companies in all situations and always involve risks for the employees concerned. such models should only be introduced under certain conditions, such as participation being voluntary and open to all employees, profit-sharing being always complementary to basic salary, the social partners being appropriately involved and the employees having a greater say in the management of the company. employee financial participation is a very good example of how we europeans can learn a lot from each other. there are many best practice examples that we as a company may not be able to copy, but we can certainly emulate. these include the sociedades laborales in spain and the stahlstiftung in austria. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council in brussels.

member of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, i would first like thank the rapporteur, ms girling. i would like to congratulate her on the eloquent way in which she laid out the reasons why honey has pollen as a constituent rather than an ingredient. this is not because the commission says so or because the court of justice says so, but because nature says so. i would also like to thank ms gabriel and the shadow rapporteurs for their active engagement on the commission’s proposal to amend the honey directive in order to determine the status of pollen as a constituent in honey. i believe it is important to provide parliament with a mandate for entering interinstitutional negotiations based not on desires, or on opinions on other matters which are only indirectly linked to this question, but simply on objective facts. i also believe this is in the interests of both consumers and beekeepers. i refer to the opinion of ms gabriel of the committee on agriculture and rural development on why it is in the interests of beekeepers to consider pollen as a constituent in honey and not as an ingredient. why should pollen be considered as a natural constituent of honey? for the very simple reason that pollen finds its way into honey as a result of the presence and activity of bees, which are so important in agriculture. you will remember that the commission only recently proposed the prohibition of certain neonicotinoids in pesticides because they were disrupting the bee population. so pollen finds its way into honey, not because the beekeeper introduces it but as a result of the presence and activities of bees. pollen is present in honey independently of the action of the beekeeper, who has no control whatsoever over the presence of pollen in the final product. pollen is therefore not a substance which is voluntarily added, like the additives which we use in food. it is not added voluntarily to the preparation of a foodstuff. it is not an ingredient. it is a natural constituent. it is precisely this that the commission’s proposal seeks to clarify. otherwise, honey would be defined as a ‘manufactured product’ rather than a primary, natural product. not only would this confuse consumers, who would think that honey is a manufactured product, but it would also be at odds with the codex alimentarius international standards, which state that no ingredient can be added to honey. so if we considered pollen to be an ingredient added to honey, that would be a violation of the rules and international standards of the codex alimentarius. i must also appeal to this assembly, as ms girling did, not to turn the commission’s proposal into a pro-gm or anti-gm issue. this proposal does not change the conclusion of the court of justice that our gmo legislation will continue to apply if gm pollen is found in honey. gm pollen in honey has to be authorised under our regulation applying to gm food and feed before it can be placed on the market. turning now to the labelling issue, which lies behind some of the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, let me stress that consumers would be informed of the presence of gm material in honey in exactly the same way as for any other food product. indeed, the same labelling rules – that is to say, labelling for above 0.9 % of the adventitious presence of gm material by ingredient – would be required as for any other foodstuff (including organic foodstuffs). lastly, let me say a few words on the comitology alignment and stress that the commission proposes delegated acts to amend only those parts of the annexes which do not contain essential elements. i therefore call on the honourable members not to remove the existing delegation granted to the commission under directive 2000/110. i hope i can count on the support of the honourable members to open the inter-institutional negotiations, which could lead us to a first-reading agreement and thus resolve this matter to the satisfaction of both honey producers and consumers.
the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the application of the 'blue card' procedure. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. you're in the liberal group, you're a liberal, and you're dealing with a lot of lobbyists. but if you say that the ingredients of milk are not listed, every time i buy a milk, it says exactly what's in it. i don't know where you get your milk. why are you going around this way? it is not a question of pollen as such, but of the manipulation of pollen by gmos. we in europe want to have natural food labelled as much as possible. are you not subject to a false lobbying influence when you represent the position you represent?
i have to say, madam president, commissioner, what you have just said is a joke for the cabaret, you could also say "pot". don't talk about what you don't know. you're talking about pollen and pollen and natural ingredients. in reality, it is about gmos, genetically modified organisms. this is the wish, this is the concern of so many beekeepers who, i think quite rightly, are bombarding us with emails at the moment saying: we want to preserve what the european court of justice has already established, namely that gmo pollen is not a natural ingredient, because it offers the possibility of actually keeping 100% gmo-free honey on the market. what you are doing is not only interfering in regulatory areas where, in the view of many citizens, the european union has nothing to lose, but you are also undermining confidence in the european union by overturning a decision of the european court of justice. the question is, of course, in whose interest? what lobbyists are you following? we follow, i follow the beekeepers of austria and other countries, you don't know. and rightly so, one must be suspicious.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the ecj clearly has no pleasure in honey if it contains pollen from genetically modified maize or other transgenic plants. that's good! the commission, however, is circumventing this judgment by proposing to classify gmo pollen as a natural component of honey and not to label it. but without the right information, consumers are not free to choose when they make a purchase. the majority of eu citizens are critical of gmos. you have a right to know if a honey contains genetically modified organisms. our local beekeepers, who produce high-quality honey, have a right to protect themselves from competition from gm products. but without labelling, it's not possible. the proposal once again favours the genetic engineering companies and importers and harms domestic consumers and ultimately small-scale beekeepers.

member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, it is true that this piece of legislation is very important in terms of the potential reduction of administrative burdens on businesses, an extension. however, confidentiality is the fundamental principle of official statistics and is recognised globally as the most important element in ensuring that businesses and citizens trust statistics and that statisticians do not start providing information to anybody who asks for this information. here – and this is very important – we are talking about information relating to individual companies: information about the trade of goods by a specific company which could be very sensitive, and that is why we consider that we should limit this possible exchange of information – as provided in the regulation – to statistical authorities and not extend it to other fields such as fiscal fields, as was mentioned by mr ngoc. on the other hand we do not have any evidence that the fiscal authorities lack statistical data. in fact, some member states have introduced systems whereby fiscal authorities participate in the collection of intrastat data through the vat information exchange system (vies) and they benefit from this, but even in this case they have to ensure very strict confidentiality regarding statistical data. that is why the commission considers that we have to stick to what it has proposed in terms of the exchange of confidential data and that such data should not be exchanged more broadly, because that might contribute to a reduction in the credibility in writing. − the rapporteur rightly points out that the south-east asian region cannot be reduced to japan, china and india alone and that significant developments have already been achieved in the areas of security, corruption and human rights. nevertheless, there is still a great deal of need for action, as human rights violations are still being committed in some countries, nuclear disarmament needs to be pushed forward and environmental protection and public safety should also be addressed more. the eu's pioneering role can provide significant political and humanitarian support, although the actual scale of its impact remains to be seen.
in writing. − by equipping long-distance lorries and buses with 'intelligent tachographs', we save time and money for those transport companies that respect driving and rest times, thus increasing road safety. with the new tachographs that can be read remotely, the often hour-long wait at road checks for shippers is finally over. i am particularly pleased about the exemption from the tachograph regulation of craft enterprises within a radius of 100 km of the company headquarters. this is an important signal to support the domestic economy!
in writing. − as traffic on europe's roads increases, there is a growing awareness of measures that can contribute to road safety. the introduction of intelligent tachographs, for example, will enable more and, above all, more precise controls. in particular, in the transit sector, road haulage is still used, for example, in respecting rest periods for drivers, which can lead to considerable traffic risks. i believe that increasing the number of cotton rolls, particularly in the transit sector, can make a significant contribution to overall road safety. more and more targeted controls by new technical systems, such as the intelligent tachograph, could put an end to manipulation. but since the draft rejects the text and would thus overturn the proposal, i voted against it. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union.
in writing. − the report by silvia-adriana ţicău deals with the issue of 'smart tachometers' and points out that they should be introduced with the aim of improving road safety and fair competition between transport companies. media reports often deal with the fact that overtired drivers are stopped after they have been well over the allowed driving time and thus pose a danger to road users. the report presented can therefore be seen as a step in the right direction, as smart tachometers are intended to prevent these circumstances. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. this is a decision to be made with due consideration. however, the precise definition of professional motorists and the strict exclusion of non-professional drivers from these checks are to be welcomed. there was no final vote on this report, only an amendment which i rejected.
in writing. − public procurement is a huge and therefore important part of the european economy. in addition, public procurement also ensures a stable situation. however, there are sectors, such as the construction industry, where there are few rules on concession levies. they are subject only to the basic provisions of the public procurement directives, and for service concessions there are rules only in the form of the general principles of the treaty and extensive case law. the result is that there is no clarification of the legal framework. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. however, i believe that the flexibility which the report highlights as a key point may once again open up too many back doors and that this could lead to another lack of transparency which the directive is intended to promote. that is why i abstained.
in writing. - fortunately, due to strong public pressure, water supply has been temporarily excluded from the scope of the concession directive. i emphasize that for the time being, because the commission has invoked a review clause and the derogations are reviewed every three years. this means that the initially planned mandatory tendering procedure in the water supply sector could soon be back on the agenda in brussels. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european network of national authorities responsible for the protection of the environment. the added value of this directive is generally questionable. municipalities will have to cope with a very complicated set of rules, for example in the area of cooperation at the municipal level. finally, the threshold for the obligation to tender is clearly too low. once again, the eu has had to bow to the pressure of the wto. i therefore could not vote for the report, while a vote against it would be equally unjustified, given the many concessions achieved through public and parliamentary pressure. there was only one abstention left.
in writing. - the concession directive was discussed at length and in a very lively manner. the commission proposal contained controversial points which parliament was able to deflect. the most important success was the exclusion of sensitive water services from the scope of the directive, not least because of the first successful european citizens' initiative right2water.eu. the complex rules governing public cooperation and public procurement have been simplified as far as possible. in addition, the principle of self-government by national, regional and local authorities was explicitly recognised in the text of the directive. the principle of freedom of design of public services is also a principle. this ensures that public services remain in the public domain. finally, binding criteria for enterprises were established: companies that receive a concession must comply with social, labour and environmental regulations. the result of the negotiations is therefore a marked improvement on the commission's draft. that is why i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. − there are compelling reasons for a legislative initiative at eu level in the field of concessions. the lack of legal certainty and the continuation of unbundled procurement in breach of the essential principles of the internal market of the european union require a clear eu legal framework.
in writing. the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of accidents. the original commission proposal has been considerably improved by rapporteur philippe juvin, so that the text now before us takes account of the specific features of concession contracts. this is a balanced approach between the flexibility of public authorities, the much-needed transparency of procurement procedures and the equal treatment of economic operators. the concession directive creates clear rules of the game and ends the fragmentation that has prevailed so far due to different national regulations. i particularly welcome the clear exclusion of water from the scope of the directive. water is a public good of public utility and as such is already regulated in article 14 of the lisbon treaty as a treaty principle. the member states have exclusive regulatory competence for the general rules on the manner in which services are provided. an important element of this subsidiary freedom of design lies in the explicit recognition of local and municipal self-government in the provision of services. this means that the decision on which services are to be licensed remains with the municipalities or the federal and state governments. the proposal for a directive never contained anything to the contrary, but many citizens have expressed fears about the alleged forced privatisation of water supply. in austria, there has been a lot of panic about this issue, which is being removed from the scope of any nutrient soil with the new, clear provisions and the explicit exception of water.
in writing. - i support this report because it aims to make the existing rules more flexible and easier to apply. the report, which is in line with the compromise reached with the council at the trilogues, will make it possible to achieve such a simplification of the rules governing public procurement.
in writing. − the revision of the public procurement directives should seek to find a middle ground between simplification of rules and effective procedures with sound award criteria. the revision is better overall, but social criteria are still lacking. there is still no possibility of taking local or national workers into account. this means that the hands of contracting authorities are still tied in some areas, especially in view of the still rigid case law of the ecj in this area. that is why i cannot agree to the report.
in writing. − public procurement accounts for almost one fifth of european gdp and is thus a major driver of the european economy. the strategic use of public expenditure is an important means of achieving social and environmental objectives. the directive aims to reform the european rules on public procurement. i voted in favour of the report because the socialist group was able to enforce mandatory social, labour and environmental criteria in the award of public contracts. it promotes companies that act socially and sustainably. this can also help to combat wage and social dumping.
in writing. − in times of crisis in the european economy, the potential of public procurement in the single market must be fully exploited. the aim is to ensure sustainable growth and employment in the future, so that the union emerges strong from the crisis. so this report can be described as a step in the right direction.
in writing. − the best way to ensure effective and socially sustainable public procurement is through approaches. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. the question is, for whom? for cheap workers from low-wage countries like bulgaria? the revision is better overall, but social criteria are still lacking. there is still no possibility of taking local or national workers into account. that is why i cannot agree to the report.
in writing. the report by marc tarabella examines the current situation in the award of public contracts and advocates a tightening of the criteria, which could benefit, among others, small and medium-sized enterprises. the commission also proposes to limit subcontracting. these approaches should lead to fairer contracting and also provide more opportunities for smes to enter and establish themselves.
in writing. − many third countries want to avoid opening up public procurement and concession markets to international competition in general or to a greater extent than has been the case so far. the actual accessibility, i.e. penetration rate, depends on a variety of factors, such as the size of the market, language barriers, technology, specialisation, etc. protectionist requirements such as the obligation to transfer technology as a condition for the award of public contracts and/or requirements relating to a domestic production share are problematic. the eu is having difficulty in getting third countries to commit themselves in this area in trade negotiations. the present report does not provide satisfactory solutions to the problems which arise, but it is not to be rejected in principle. that is why i abstained.
in writing. - opening up the market to third countries and offering public contracts and concessions to international competition is commonplace in our time. the developing countries must not be the losers in this regulation. in any case, the matter should be approached with caution, in order to act in the spirit of the common commercial policy. the final vote has been postponed.
in writing. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of genetically modified organisms (gmos) in the production of food. the fact that in future it will not be possible for consumers to identify on the label whether honey contains pollen from genetically modified plants, because the legal construction of the labelling obligation is too controversial, is grotesque. finally, it is important that consumers are informed.
in writing. the report considers pollen to be an ingredient, which means that there is no labelling requirement for genetically modified pollen. consumer protection must be a priority in this matter. the labelling of honey containing genetically modified pollen must be visible to the consumer. in order to maintain european standards in the field of consumer protection and food quality, i am voting against this report.
in writing. − according to the judgment of the european court of justice of 6 september 2011 in case c-442/09, pollen from genetically modified plants is to be considered as an ingredient of honey or food supplements containing pollen within the meaning of regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 of the european parliament and of the council. the commission now proposed in its proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council directive 2001/110/ec on honey that 'pollen is a component of honey which does not contain any ingredients as a natural substance'. according to this reasoning, genetically modified pollen should also be considered as a natural component of honey. this is not acceptable to consumers or to beekeepers who produce a natural, high-quality product. i therefore supported the proposal of the committee on the environment, which is committed to the interests of beekeepers and consumers.
in writing. - i abstained because the majority of the amendments which were critical (including the one on gmo pollen) were adopted. the final vote has been postponed.
in writing. - our aim must be to prevent subsidy fraud from the outset. this requires not only stricter sanctions but also a consistent simplification of the rules, as has already been done, in order to close loopholes which fraudsters can exploit all too easily. it is of course important in this context to continue the hercule anti-fraud programme to promote anti-fraud training and technical and scientific support. the european commission's continued push for the creation of an eu prosecutor is, however, a matter of concern. i have incorporated these considerations into my voting behaviour.
in writing. the 'hercule iii' programme is designed to promote action in the field of the protection of the european union's financial interests. the following priority areas will be given special attention: cigarette smuggling, trade in counterfeit cigarettes, corruption and fraud and other illegal activities. the commission will also be able to take account of the need to ensure that the rules are not overlapping and that duplicate work is avoided. the overall financial allocation for the implementation of the programme is eur 110 million for the period 2014-2020, but the author stresses the importance of greater budgetary discipline. the report is to be welcomed in this sense, since the financial security of the european union and its citizens is important.
in writing. − the rapporteur points out that increased data exchange can improve the quality of european statistics. however, it should be noted that the cost savings sought should not be over-emphasised, as they may be used in the wrong places. neither privacy nor security should be neglected when exchanging confidential data, and at this point, cost savings should be carefully weighed.
in writing. − the illegal trade in products of protected species is a thriving business, estimated to generate at least $19 billion in annual sales worldwide. it serves as a source of revenue for a global criminal network and thus also promotes the support of militant rebel groups, especially in africa. it is also feared that the hunting of certain already scarce species will soon be unable to prevent their extinction. the other aspects of these crimes are political unrest, threats to the security of some countries and their economies, and not least the deprivation of local livelihoods. i believe that there is no question that poaching and crimes against wildlife and protected species should be prosecuted and punished severely. the reality, however, is that the rulers of many of the countries concerned are making too much money from this form of trade and have little interest in putting a stop to it. i am afraid that the measures proposed by the eu may prove to be ineffective as long as there is no successful cooperation with these countries and the horse is reared once again from behind, so i have abstained.
in writing. - it is essential that the penalties for offences against wild fauna and flora should be increased. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. the eu should act in unison in this area and impose stronger penalties, which should also be carried out in consultation with non-eu countries. in addition, the citizens of the union should be informed and made aware of the seriousness of the offences in this area.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i have to go. i am now dealing with the implementation of community law for the fifth time in the form of this report and i can only repeat and emphasize that the implementation of what we decide here in lengthy procedures, discuss and then fix in council negotiations, should be of central importance to us. we shouldn't just ignore it. unfortunately, many people are simply satisfied when they see that i have been part of a beautiful law. whether this law is then applied and whether it is then also applied correctly is actually the question that must concern us in two respects: firstly, the appreciation and the need for european standards and secondly, we in the legislature also need a feedback loop to improve our legislative work. and what else can tell us about this than non-implementation or infringement procedures? in the last year - we have got statistics here - the number of infringement procedures initiated by the commission when member states fail to implement has continued to fall. there are now some 1770 procedures. there is also a hierarchy of laws that are implemented least well or not at all. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. how can the commission tell that there are massive deficits here? if there are complainants or if she herself is made aware of it or is made aware of it. the number of complaints i mentioned earlier is not all of them. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are not undermined. but we don't know how well or how badly the implementation control will work in the end. why not? - why not? there is a gigantic lack of transparency within the commission. there is a so-called pilot procedure in which the commission and the member state concerned deal with a case of non-implementation, but the complainant is not informed. we in parliament do not know which areas have the greatest implementation deficits. we have been working for five years to improve this situation and we are again calling on the commission to introduce a procedure, a novelty, so that this becomes a regulated procedure, so that the complainant, so that the parliamentarians have access to anonymised information. we don't want to overturn privacy, but we want to know how well we make laws here. this is a central point for me and i would like to stress it. the second point, mr karim, on better lawmaking, i would just like to make two brief comments. i think he is going a little too far on the question of subsidiarity control by member states. if we go as far as karim suggests, we will again have veto powers in the council, which will then block essential legislation for certain reasons, and often just to achieve something else. secondly, i think that there is too much overestimation of impact assessments. we have seen impact assessments ourselves where substantial pieces of information were not checked by the commission, but only those parts which justified the commission's position. but that is the wrong way to go, in my view!

answer to a question on the 'blue card' procedure. madam president, i am very much in favour of respect for fundamental rights at national and european level. and just as we are committed to ensuring that they are respected at national level, we are also committed to ensuring that the rights enshrined in the european charter of fundamental rights are respected.
i have to say, madam president, theoretically, as you know, we have the principle of subsidiarity, which is intended to prevent the union from declaring itself competent at all times and in all places. in the course of the last few years, however, we have seen a massive transfer of competence to brussels through various back doors. if we look at the united kingdom, for example, there is a lot of buzz about the application of eu law and the european convention on human rights. critics are right to say that the country has never accepted that decisions important to the social and political order are taken by international courts that are not accountable. and if the european court of justice has the last word in fundamental rights and the ecj has always acted as an instrument to give brussels more powers, then in my view this is also a form of machinery for transferring powers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union is able to meet its obligations under the treaty. i think it is high time that we in the union finally made it clear that under the cloak of freedom of movement and solidarity not everything can be allowed!

of who you share your life with? the european union has strategies to combat discrimination against roma people, discrimination against people with disabilities. this parliament has already asked the affairs decided to go ahead and demand it, because we know the situation is grave. the fundamental rights agency of the european union made clear in a report involving a questionnaire that 93 000 lgbt people answered last year that 60% are afraid at times to walk hand-in-hand in the street. almost 50% are harassed or discriminated against and one in four has been physically attacked or threatened with violence in the previous five years. that is homophobia, and it must no longer be tolerated in europe. so many of us – lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and inter-sex people – have lived our lives in fear for too long. my report says that we must act on this. and it is not about telling member states or about breaching the competences of member states. we have made that very clear in paragraph 5. you can all read it: ‘this comprehensive policy must respect the competences of the european union, of its agencies, and of member states’. but we need to act on that. this report tells the commission – this commission and the next – and it tells us, in this year’s election campaign, that we have to work on fighting fear, on making sure that people who are harassed or attacked because they are lesbian or gay will go to the police, that they will have police officers there who understand what the problem is, and that they are not harassed again. and it should make sure that, for example, schools in member states share best practices with regard to talking about the fact that lgbt people and families exist on this continent and they should not be discriminated against anymore.

member of the commission. - madam president, today is international day against female genital mutilation (fgm). it is an opportunity to remind the world that the european union condemns this abhorrent crime. it is our legal and human obligation to protect women and girls, both within and outside the european union, from the risks of mutilation. i welcome this initiative by the european parliament to hold a debate on the subject. female genital mutilation is a brutal manifestation of gender inequality and a violation of human rights. on several occasions, this parliament has called on the commission to act ambitiously. the commission and the european union as a whole are committed to a strengthened policy response to combat all forms of violence against women within the union territory and in our external relations. this is demonstrated in the commission’s action plan implementing the stockholm programme, the women’s charter and the commission’s strategy for equality between women and men. the commission is working to improve knowledge and data collection and to prevent violence. this is being achieved through awareness raising and exchanges of good practice and by providing funding to governments, ngos and networks active in this field. the commission’s most recent sign of commitment was the adoption on 25 november 2013 of its communication on eliminating female genital mutilation. fgm is also a form of child abuse. it is estimated that currently 500 000 women and girls in the european union alone may have suffered from this harmful practice. this parliament calls for a specific strategy and an action plan on violence against women. i would like to emphasise that all the commission initiatives and measures are mutually complementary and that they already constitute a solid and comprehensive framework for concrete action, bringing tangible results and making full use of eu competences to support the member states in eliminating all forms of violence against women. fgm is a very specific form of violence: it reflects a deep-rooted social norm; it is often practised in the belief that it is beneficial for the girl; and it is an intimate issue and still, in many case, a taboo subject. it is crucial to take into account its complexities. that is why the commission adopted its action plan on fgm, following parliament’s resolution in 2012. let me now address the question of european union legislative action. we have made significant progress in adopting concrete legislative proposals in the field of criminal and civil justice to support women against violence. this includes: the directive on trafficking in human beings; the directive against sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography; the directive on the european protection order applicable in criminal matters, complemented by a regulation applicable in civil matters; and the directive on the rights of crime victims. this legislation emphasises the need for specific and appropriate protection for victims of gender-based violence. we have a comprehensive legal framework at european level to protect women against all forms of violence. this framework needs to be effectively implemented by member states at national level. the commission is assisting them in this respect and will monitor effective implementation. in addition, as i mentioned earlier, there is a series of non-legislative measures: awareness-raising, exchanges of good practice and funding. those measures already contribute to supporting member states in preventing the violence. as regards external relations policy, i reiterate that human rights, democracy and the rule of law are inherent in our analysis when it comes to assessing whether – and what type of – budget support is appropriate in a given country. women’s and girls’ rights are, of course, part of this. the european union is also taking its first steps towards developing and applying a human-rights-based approach in development cooperation. civil society organisations are recognised as fully-fledged actors and partners for development. when it comes to fgm in particular, the european union has, for many years, been participating actively in international cooperation initiatives to promote the elimination of fgm. the union systematically raises the issue of fgm in its dialogues with african, caribbean and pacific countries and underlines the need for african states to ensure that the practice is effectively prohibited. the european union supports capacity-building for government officials and advocacy and awareness-raising for all sectors of society, and it is preparing a regional campaign on fgm, which will be carried out by its delegations in third countries in 2014. the european union also funds projects. from 2006 to 2012, 17 projects addressing fgm in 18 countries benefited from eu funding of approximately eur 8 million. for example, an innovative eu and unicef project has contributed to changing attitudes towards fgm in egypt, eritrea, ethiopia, senegal and sudan. additionally, through the european instrument for democracy and human rights (eidhr), the eu has supported several important projects run by human rights ngos in this area.

if we are to promote and preserve these waterways at all, with less navigability in the rivers, then we must look more closely at this. i ask you, have you done it, or will you do it?

european issues. we are seeing more and more examples where the council – the ministers – are saying no, of course, we agree on the substance, but we the ministers want to do it. this means that we have to explain to our citizens, to the audience up here, that these decisions are very often not efficient, because to come to an agreement in the council – although there are only 28 members – is the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's air transport system is not affected by the crisis. for more than 26 million passengers who take off and land in austria alone each year, there will be more and faster compensation and simplified complaint procedures for delays and cancellations. passengers who are delayed for more than three hours have the same rights as passengers whose flight has been cancelled. this means that you will receive compensation of up to 300 euros for flights up to 3 500 km, and up to 600 euros for long-haul flights. the handbag harassment of some low-cost airlines has also come to an end. the maximum size and weight of the total hand baggage allowance per passenger will now be specified. the number of pieces of luggage may no longer be limited. the burdensome complaint procedures often prevent passengers from exercising their rights. we therefore now require airlines to set up information and assistance points at air terminals.

in writing. - the negotiating directives for a readmission agreement between the european community and turkey were adopted by the council on 28 november 2002. in may 2005, the negotiations were officially opened in brussels. this agreement is very important for turkey to take back people from the eu. the resumption is linked to the visa liberalisation roadmap with turkey (visa-free travel); turkey signed the agreement on 16 december 2013, after the visa liberalisation roadmap was introduced. the obligation to take back one's own national also extends to family members (spouses and minor unmarried children) irrespective of their nationality who do not have an independent right of residence in the requesting state. the readmission obligation for third-country nationals or stateless persons is subject to a number of preconditions and does not apply until three years after the entry into force of the entire convention.
in the case of the turkish border, the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the turkish border is not crossed by any other border. turkey is thus the main transit country for illegal immigration into the european union. the readmission agreement would make an important contribution to curbing illegal immigration to the european union via the territory of turkey. at the same time, it would contribute to the fight against crossborder crime, in particular trafficking in human beings, and would lead to a significant relief for greece and thus for the european union as a whole. in order to make it possible to return migrants who have entered the european union illegally, i am voting in favour of this agreement with turkey.
in the case of the turkish authorities, the commission has not yet taken a decision on the application of the principle of non-refoulement. the rapporteur also condemns the uncompromising attitude of turkey, which is now linking its signature to the agreement to visa liberalization and thus wants to put pressure on the european union. the return agreement should be considered, but it would also involve significant financial support, as the agreement would provide turkey with financial and technical assistance from the european union for the establishment of border police and border surveillance equipment. in view of the human rights situation in turkey - a candidate country which has not committed itself to complying with the binding copenhagen political criteria for the pre-accession phase since it obtained this status - it should be carefully considered whether additional financial resources should be allocated to this country.
in the future, the final votes at committee level will be taken by name by the members. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i believe that this innovation was long overdue, since it will finally bring more transparency to the work of the european parliament. the computer system now records the name of each participating member and whether he or she voted for or against a proposal or abstained. the amendment also requires a roll-call vote in plenary for non-binding resolutions. at present, this procedure is mandatory only for legislative decisions; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the railways are able to operate across europe without technical or bureaucratic obstacles. the ppp has voted for efficient, fast, low-cost and service-oriented rail transport. the aim of travelling from gdansk to venice via vienna with a single train and a single ticket will only become a reality if the old monopolists are forced to cooperate. i believe that competition in the railway market is essential to make rail transport more attractive. our transport policy of switching from road to rail will only succeed if rail becomes even more efficient and service-oriented, especially in passenger transport. this requires fair competition, europeanisation and the approximation of technical standards. what good is the eu if the air conditioning in the carriage stops working on a train heading for the border and the italian railway company can prohibit austrian trains from stopping at mestre? national monopolies, different types of electricity, different safety standards and track gauges are a relic of the last century and are now being abolished once and for all.
in writing. - although the commission's proposal was improved in many respects by the report voted on today, i abstained in the final vote because i do not agree in principle with the commission's 'one size fits all' approach. there is no link between the structure of the railway undertaking and the railway's market share or customer satisfaction. on the contrary, the most successful railways in passenger transport are integrated railways. the different regional characteristics of the member states should be taken into account more closely and a uniform (separate) company structure should not be prescribed. interoperability and the development of international rail links are much more important for the european railway area.
in the case of the railways, the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the railway system is not affected by the introduction of new technologies. under the pretext of liberalization, there is a threat of overbureaucratization for smaller railway companies. the present package will make it virtually impossible to operate public transport services for general use without a profit maximisation approach. the municipalities are deprived of the possibility of compensating for losses incurred by their local transport undertaking by means of profits made by other municipal undertakings. this naturally has a negative impact on the provision of services by bus and rail. public operators will face eu-wide competition on the few profitable routes, while there will be little international interest in the less interesting and loss-making secondary routes. the fourth railway package threatens to destroy the secondary lines and regional railways. the rural regions are particularly affected, as their infrastructure is becoming increasingly depleted.
in writing. - the 4th railway package is designed to promote the integration of european rail transport. the main elements are a mandatory eu-wide tender instead of a direct public procurement, more separation within a railway company between the individual sub-operations, such as network and operation, and a central european approval authority (era) for railway matters. this is to increase competition and increase safety. so much for the theory, because we have heard the same stories in the postal, energy and telecommunications sectors, and reality has often shown something else. the railway companies of smaller eu member states will be particularly affected. these have few profitable routes and are now also competing with giants such as db and sncf, which have much larger financial resources. at the same time, cross-subsidisation is now much more difficult, i.e. how can öbb's non-profit routes, which are operated in the public interest, continue to be financed without incurring debt? surpluses from grid operation may no longer be transferred to running lines. competition would not harm öbb, but not too much and not too quickly, otherwise the costly failure of the öbb rescue could result for the taxpayer. that's why i voted against the fourth railway package.
in writing. - the report presented on the unification of the european railway area considers that the performance of the railway sector should be significantly increased. in this context, it is committed to the creation of a transit ticket, the fight against social dumping in respect of employees and passenger rights. however, it should be carefully considered whether the point concerning the retention of passenger data should be accepted, as this system is very similar to the backup of passenger data and should be carefully considered with regard to data protection.
in writing. - the rapporteur was able to reach a compromise with the majority of the groups on the key elements of the report: direct award, open access and competitive award procedures, the principle of reciprocity (internal and vis-à-vis third countries), the content of the transport plan (with clear criteria on efficiency and quality requirements), the role of the competent authority (regional and also local), information and under- and overcompensation, the scope of public service contracts (options for small and large member states: small states can be covered by a single public service contract and the larger the market, the greater the number of contracts to be awarded), the use of rolling stock and transit time. the committee therefore supported measures to limit the scope of public service contracts and to promote increased competition in this sector.
in writing. - there is no link between the degree of liberalisation and the quality and efficiency of the railway system. further liberalisation of the railways will only lead to the 'picking of raisins' on profitable routes and to profits for a few large companies. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information it receives. i therefore voted against the grosch report on principle, although i recognize that the socialist group has been able to achieve some important improvements for workers.
in writing. - the report presented deals with the unification of the railway sector and the interoperability of the railway system. the rapporteur is in favour of opening up the sector and against the fragmentation of the railway sector. the time taken for a new company to establish itself should be reduced. the main aim is to adopt the third railway package to make the fourth package possible.
in writing. - the report by the greens/efa rapporteur is ambitious and contains provisions for the future european railway sector, under which the european railway agency is the only authority to issue safety certificates and is the last resort for national safety authorities dealing with national safety rules. in close alignment with the interoperability directive, the compromise solutions relate to the role of the era as the authority responsible for issuing individual safety certificates (depending on the field of application); clearly defined division of responsibilities and relationship between the era and the nsas, deadlines to be applied in the application procedure; the use of languages; social provisions on rest periods and the creation of conditions that facilitate the reporting of safety risks by staff.
in writing. - the report deals with railway safety, an important issue because railway accidents are very rare but have devastating consequences. in this sense, the report is to be welcomed, as the rapporteur is in favour of increased cooperation between all stakeholders in the railway sector and also believes that it should be possible to report concerns anonymously to the national safety agencies. the report is therefore to be welcomed, even if it is necessary to consider whether the issuing of safety certificates should actually be accelerated, as this could be at the expense of safety.
in writing. - the report presented by robert zīle mainly deals with the different conditions for safety authorizations and certificates in the various eu member states. this illustrates the need for action in this area in particular if the railway sector is to be made more attractive and, above all, more competitive. the report is to be welcomed in this sense, since its author is critical of the unequal competition and calls for action to be taken to combat it.
in writing. - the report presented is entirely to be supported, since it concerns compensation which should be equally available to all railway undertakings and therefore the repeal of regulation (eec) no 1192/69 is entirely justified. however, an early repeal of the regulation could have negative consequences and therefore the opposite effect.
in writing. - the report by christine de veyrac deals with the reporting of events in civil aviation and stresses the urgent need for action in this area, as it is assumed that air traffic will increase steadily and significantly. since most occurrence reports are made by aviation workers, these new protective measures are intended to protect them from sanctions or consequences of their reports. the report also calls for the collection of data in a database, which is a welcome approach, but nonetheless requires special attention to data protection. in this respect the report is to be welcomed and can be voted in favour.
in writing. - i support the rapporteur's view that the proposal for a decision on the introduction of the interoperable eu-wide ecall service is welcome and that the objective is to ensure the coordinated and coherent introduction of the interoperable eu-wide ecall service and to ensure interoperability and continuity of the service throughout europe. this is in line with the position of the european parliament, which has repeatedly - including in its resolution on the ecall service - reaffirmed its support for the introduction of the ecall system. the report on a new 112 service for citizens was adopted by a large majority in july 2012; in this report, the rapporteur and therefore the epp group regrets the delays and lack of progress in the voluntary introduction of ecall and urges the commission to propose the regulatory measures necessary to avoid further delays.
in writing. - while the report has made important improvements in the data protection aspects of ecall, the electronics of ecall remain a latent threat. every car is now technologically equipped to be a data transmitter. the citizen has no choice. then it's just a small step to lucrative and governmental surveillance options: insurance companies crave data to personalize contracts, the emergence of various ancillary services with vehicle tracking, secret services that don't follow the law and rules, creation of movement profiles and metadata. saving lives is a noble goal, but it seems that little has been learned from the nsa scandal. this is where the technological foundation is being laid for monitoring the movements of our citizens. a clear yes to saving lives, but also a yes to ecall volunteering. i have therefore abstained from voting on this balance between the clear benefits of ecall and the risks it entails.
in the case of the european parliament, the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information it receives. in principle, this approach is very commendable, but this report should not be accepted lightly without considering that automated technology could be used as a basis for a pan-european surveillance infrastructure. the data protection issue is an important aspect which cannot be ignored, especially in view of the recent media reports on mass data storage.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report as, in my opinion, it offers a wider protection to customer interests and needs. the objective of the european commission proposal on ‘insurance mediation’ is to improve and make conditions of the retail insurance market more efficient and in the interest of the end consumer. the consumers of insurance products would receive better advice and information on the existing insurance products that they would need and, more than that, insurance services will be less complicated as less burdensome rules on free provision and establishment of these services will be introduced. the final vote was postponed.
in writing. - the €60 million health for growth programme is part of the europe 2020 strategy. it is intended to promote innovation in healthcare and ensure its sustainability. some of the approaches in the programme may be good, such as some coordination and exchange of information at eu level. however, health is a national competence and should remain so. that is why i abstained.
in this report the rapporteur sets out the main challenges facing the union in the social and health sectors in the years to come. research and innovation play as important a role here as adequate health standards and prevention. with an ageing population, prevention is particularly important to maintain people's living standards and to keep the social costs as low as possible. the training of qualified staff and the creation of sufficient places and jobs round off this approach. i would like to emphasize the passages on alzheimer's and dementia. these neurodegenerative diseases will increase even more in the future and will place a great burden on society, on family members and on the health system. i support the report's call for preventive action and remedial action to be taken in good time.

in writing. - the aim of today's parliamentary resolution is to achieve a europe-wide internet speed of 1 gigabit per second in at least half of all households and 100 megabit per second in austria by 2020. if we do not succeed in connecting the rural areas of austria to high-power networks, we will be entering a dangerous spiral of further economic separation between the countryside and the urban centre. only if public co-financing rates are high can more private money be mobilised for infrastructure development. in addition, private-public partnerships and tax incentives for network expansion are needed. unfortunately, the eu still lags behind the us, japan and south korea in terms of average broadband speed.

in writing. - the report's concept covers all the principles and techniques to ensure 'accessible access' to public websites for all users. the concept includes the content of a website, web browsers and technologies such as a screen reader. the proposal should ensure that websites are more easily accessible to people with disabilities and older people. the term 'public authorities' covers, for example, the state, local authorities and bodies governed by public law. the total estimated cost of implementation is approximately eur 2 billion. however, what the objectives of this report do not reflect is the user's perspective. the question to be asked here is: what is the benefit of the directive and does it lead to an improvement in the living conditions of the citizens? i have abstained on this vote because of some weaknesses in the report.
in writing. - the rapporteur considers that there is a need to increase the accessibility of public sector websites. the report is also very welcome, as mr chatzimarkakis points out that the measures envisaged do not go far enough and that technical developments in mobile data carriers must be taken into account. since disabled people also need to be guaranteed the same access to public bodies' websites and services, this report should be adopted.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report because in my view we have to support long-term investments all over europe, as a help strategy for the european economy and its recovery. i believe that we need more investment; we need more long-term investments for the private sector. we have to assist smes in order to activate the ‘economic engine’. everybody knows that a well-functioning economy has a business environment that also functions very well and this means that access to financing for smes has to be facilitated. we need to create an ‘efficient economic infrastructure’ that will foster sustainable growth and jobs in the long term and that will ensure an economically stable future for our young generation.
in writing. - i see the following problems in this report: the definition of prostitution as a violation of human rights, a violation of human dignity and slavery and thus incompatible with the eu charter of fundamental rights. the portrayal of prostitution as a criminal act. equating prostitution with forced prostitution. the presentation of the nordic model (punishing those who use the services of sex workers) as the only solution to curb prostitution, forced prostitution and sexual exploitation. in austria, as in other member states, prostitution is legal and subject to national regulations. in order to deal with these problems in the best possible way, i voted against the epp line on several points, which supports some of the above points, and i voted accordingly in the free votes. i am very clear about the need to combat illegal prostitution, human trafficking, forced prostitution and sexual exploitation. but it is important to respect legal prostitution, which is regulated differently in the member states, and to draw attention to the principle of subsidiarity.
in writing. - the report presented looks at the development of responsible business practices in developing countries. as these are often rich in raw materials, corporate practices that are sometimes in breach of human rights lead to conflict and exploitation of civil society. in this sense, the report by judith sargentini can only be welcomed, as the rapporteur is committed to fair business practices and also points out that transnational companies should be encouraged to adopt responsible practices. the rapporteur's criticisms are appropriate and the report can be accepted.

the next item is the joint debate on the report by nuno melo, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on the european investigation order in criminal matters (09288/2010[nbsp]-[nbsp]c7-0185/2010[nbsp]-[nbsp]2010/0817(cod)) (a7-0477/2013) and the report with recommendations to the commission by sarah ludford, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the review of the european arrest warrant (2013/2109(lin)) (http://www.europarl.europa.eu/sides/get.dooc?type=pre&tor=reference-2014-a3900l=de&l=" \tanguage"_blank" ).
i have to say, madam president, the european investigation order is a very important law in the field of police and judicial cooperation which will be adopted tomorrow. it is also an important step towards the implementation of the stockholm programme objectives. it is also worth noting that the initiative was not taken by the commission but by seven member states, including austria, the country i represent here in the european parliament. this shows once again that national and european interests are not in conflict. this is also primarily related to the fact that security added value can be achieved in this way. the inquiry order will significantly facilitate and improve cross-border prosecution in europe, as many of the current obstacles to mutual legal assistance can be removed. the inquiry order introduces automation between eu countries, making crossborder investigations faster and more effective. who should be against it? the value of such a tool cannot be underestimated, as it has often been bureaucratic obstacles that have hindered or complicated police investigations. this cannot and must not be in the interests of citizens who have a right to personal security. at the same time, we must be aware that the field of law enforcement and investigation is a highly sensitive one and that great care must be taken to ensure that the fundamental rights of the accused are respected. the protection of fundamental rights and their enshrinement in law is therefore of fundamental importance. i am very pleased that in the negotiations with the council we have succeeded in introducing a fundamental rights clause in article 10. an inquiry order may only be issued if the fundamental rights of the person concerned under the eu charter of fundamental rights and the eu treaty are not affected. in addition, we were able to ensure in articles 5 and 10 that only measures of inquiry which are also permitted under national law in the member state concerned may be applied. the investigation order has thus been placed at important limits. it is a successful attempt to prevent abuse. with our changes to the european investigation order, we as the european parliament are showing that the protection of fundamental rights and enhanced police and judicial cooperation in europe are compatible. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr melo, and all the shadow rapporteurs for their good and intensive work.

in writing. - today's vote is a victory for youth and health care. despite the new stricter rules, there will be no expansive packaging regulation. shocking images and warnings will make up 65 percent of the front and back of cigarette packs. eu countries now have 24 months to transpose the directive into national law. tobacco use is the greatest preventable health risk. smoking kills nearly 700,000 people in europe each year. about 94 percent of all smokers start before the age of 25. the austrian pharmacy association estimates that smoking causes up to 14,000 deaths a year in austria alone. the aim is not to restrict the freedom of self-determination of people, but to point out the risks involved. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a new definition of the term 'smoking'. tobacco is supposed to taste like tobacco. the introduction of additives such as vanilla and menthol should not make smoking more palatable. these practices of the tobacco industry, which deliberately attract young people, are therefore prohibited from 2017 and 2020 respectively. it is right to do whatever is necessary to discourage young people from entering.
in writing. - although in principle it is welcome that smoking and the negative health effects of smoking are brought to the fore and that additives are examined more closely. the european commission is going too far in its campaign against smokers. it is disproportionate to impose such a degree of control on tobacco companies over the design of their products. neither warnings nor massive tax increases will stop our youths from starting to smoke. this requires a social rethinking, which is already under way even without the brussels gangs. as regards the electronic cigarette, i think that this subject should have been dealt with in a separate directive, since it is obviously not a tobacco product.
in writing. - the tobacco products directive is to be rejected for several reasons: first of all, it should be noted that there are already enough warning labels on tobacco products. the fact that the eu is forcing such detailed harmonisation proves once again how much it meddles in the little things of everyday life: it cannot solve big problems like the crisis in ukraine. but the display of a pack of cigarettes is a matter of state. secondly, i am opposed to this directive because it interferes with the private autonomy of citizens. it is not possible to prove that shock images on cigarette packs actually deter smoking. it is therefore not justified to prohibit manufacturers from representing an established trade mark on the packaging of a tobacco product. i am a firm non-smoker, just as i am convinced that the freedom of citizens must be protected at all costs. the directive in question must also be rejected because i cannot in any way endorse the image of the eu as a consumer, which has in mind a minor citizen whose consumption the eu wants to standardise in european law. it is regrettable that the european parliament has given its approval to this body of rules.
in writing. - smoking is the leading cause of death that could have been avoided. it kills about 700,000 people a year. the average smoker in europe is 28%, while in latvia it is 36%. in europe, it is second only to greece! although the eu adopted the tobacco products directive 12 years ago and the number of smokers has fallen since then, the rate is still critically high. smoking among young people is particularly troubling. statistics show that 29% of young people aged 15-25 smoke - more than the population as a whole. smoking has a negative impact on public health and increases healthcare costs. i therefore supported the directive, which provides for targeted action to make tobacco products less attractive, thereby reducing the number of young people who turn to smoking, such as the ban on cigarettes and tobacco 'garts' and 'mazo' packs containing less than 20 cigarettes. it is also important to increase the warning requirements for smoking hazards to 65% on both the front and rear surfaces. the market for e-cigarettes has been completely unregulated until now. with the new directive, e-cigarettes sold as a means of smoking cessation will be subject to the same rules as medicines. in other cases, they will be regulated in the same way as tobacco products, and in these cases the nicotine concentration will not exceed 20 mg/ml.

it means that the guarantee will allow the european investment bank to scale up eu investment in ukraine, for example, to invest in critical infrastructure. it will allow the european investment bank to continue investing in north africa following the arab spring, including investment to promote growth and create jobs. the european union guarantee will also allow the european investment bank to continue complementing other eu operations more globally in pre-accession countries in the neighbourhood area and also in asia and latin america. moreover, the proposed decision reinforces the cooperation between the bank, the commission and the european external action service and further enhances transparency and promotes broad stakeholder consultation on european investment bank operations. the eib will promote eu policies whilst managing its operations in accordance with the principles of sound banking practices. the eu guarantee will complement the eib’s own risk operations and will add value by supporting local private sector development, in particular by providing support to smes through the development of social and economic infrastructure, including transport, energy and environmental infrastructure and information and communication technology, and through investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation.

in writing. we are voting tomorrow on a little-noticed subject which could have far-reaching consequences. the so-called fluorinated gases - i.e. refrigerants, solvents, insulating gases, foam propellants and aerosol propellants - used in a wide range of industrial sectors are to be replaced in the long term by climate-friendly alternatives. why would you do that? fluorinated gases contribute up to a thousand times more to global warming than co2. their use increased steadily when cfcs and other ozone-depleting substances were banned by the montreal protocol in the 1980s. in 2011, the share of 'f-gases' in the eu-15 greenhouse gas emissions was already 2.2%. with the expected increase in demand for refrigerants in developing and emerging countries, more and more fluorinated gases are expected to enter the atmosphere and heat the climate over the next decades. i therefore support the compromise for a phased-out timetable, which would prohibit particularly climate-damaging f-gases in stationary refrigeration systems from 2022 and in stationary air conditioning systems from 2025. we have also introduced a review clause for the pricing and auctioning of allowances. in the interests of our climate, i would therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to vote in favour of this compromise. thank you, sir.
in writing. the directive to facilitate the exercise of the rights of mobile workers in the eu is an important step towards creating fairer and more transparent conditions. we cannot accept that workers who work in another eu country than their own are worse off than their own citizens. the principle of 'equal pay for equal work at the same place' must always apply. this directive brings some important improvements, such as easier access to information and legal support for mobile workers. it is particularly important to me that the strong role of the social partners and the need to respect collective agreements have been highlighted. in the same breath, reference should be made to safety and health at work and the need for effective labour controls to ensure that the law is enforced accordingly. my demand that employers provide comprehensible wage statements and working time records in the event of a court case was not accepted in the negotiations with the council. nevertheless, the new directive brings clear improvements for the workers concerned, including the so-called frontier workers. in addition, member states still have room to create the most favourable conditions for mobile workers as they implement the directive.

in writing. - the age of existing regulations and the revelations of nsa interceptions have made it too late to refocus and revise data protection in the eu. the amendments proposed in the report are the result of a long struggle against massive (us) lobbying and for the citizens. the level of data protection is being raised de facto, oversight and control opportunities for citizens are being improved with uniform standards, surveillance is being left to national authorities and strong penalties are being introduced for infringements by companies. this is only a small part of the innovations. in essence, it was a mammoth achievement to create a flexible law that also takes into account the continuous innovations in this innovative business environment, and to set a clear and hard line that cannot be interpreted at will. i think the rapporteur has succeeded to a large extent in this. the nsa scandal and its consequences were also taken into account in the text of the law. i therefore voted in favour of the report.
