the commission has already made a number of proposals. we did it and we kept our word. today marks the adoption of a major project in response to the experience of the crisis, the next major step in european integration and the establishment of an important insurance policy for european citizens. the banking union is our insurance against the taxpayer being taken advantage of in the event of bank failures. we are making europe's banks more stable and more resilient. the new capital rules create rules and standards for all european banks. joint supervision at the ecb ensures that rules are applied in the same way everywhere. there is a rapid reaction capability through 'testaments' for all banks under the bank insolvency law. at the same time, we are creating more security for retail investors by quickly withdrawing the protected eur 100 000 within seven days. the deposit guarantee fund is being set up. bail-in in the event of insolvency is becoming the norm, and we are starting to set up a bank resolution fund. one of the main objectives of our efforts is therefore secured: no more use of taxpayers' money to rescue banks. commissioner, we have also adopted the banker boni scheme as part of the implementation of basel iii. on 4 march 2014, they submitted a delegated regulation setting out detailed criteria for identifying risk holders covered by this restriction. we as legislators have set clear rules and we demand that the supervisory authorities and the european commission do everything possible to implement them consistently. this includes, in our view, that if a bank considers that a person is not a risk-taker within the meaning of the regulation, an ex-ante emergency notification must be sent to the competent authorities. the commission's proposal raises a great deal of questions for us in this respect. we do not want loopholes, we do not tolerate loopholes. we want the banker-bonus system to be implemented one-on-one, and that is why i am asking you to make a statement and to take a clear position so that this question mark can be cleared up.

in writing. - this directive, which has been under discussion since 2005 and can finally be implemented with the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, will bring more flexibility and security to european workers. it has long been possible within the eu to 'take legal pension rights with you to another member state'. the directive now extends this to supplementary pension rights, such as occupational pensions. cash reimbursements for balances in supplementary pension accounts, however small, are only permitted with the explicit consent of the persons concerned. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive. the rules will have to be implemented from 2018 and will therefore continue to contribute to the free movement of persons within the eu.
in writing. - the commission's proposal for legislation on animal health is intended to replace some 40 different eu legislation in this area, some of which is outdated. the proposal aims to create a single, simplified, transparent and clear regulatory framework, which allows for a clear and balanced distribution of tasks and responsibilities between the competent authorities of the member states, the eu institutions, the agricultural sector, animal owners, etc. in the monitoring, prevention and control of various animal diseases. this includes the principle that prevention is better than cure and that veterinary medicinal products must be used responsibly. the proposal focuses on the prevention and control of animal diseases transmissible to animals or humans. animal welfare is of enormous importance for animals, but also for public health, as about 70% of infectious diseases affect both animals and humans. that is why i voted in favour of the report.

in writing. - the report suggests that, due to the ineffectiveness of the 1993 directive, the same committee should continue to be responsible for monitoring the implementation of the directive and that member states should report on the implementation of the revised directive within approximately three years of its adoption. this amendment is necessary to enable the member states and the commission, together with the european parliament, to discuss ways of implementing the objectives of the directive more effectively. the report also contains amendments relating to the internal market information system and clarifying the need to comply with data protection rules.
in the case of the united kingdom, the commission has already taken the initiative in the form of a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. the european clarification of the return of illegally transferred cultural goods is also important in view of european history and its impact up to the present day.
in the next three years, eu member states must halve the consumption of plastic bags, but they can choose how to do it. this is an important step for our environment, our health, our landscape and for conserving resources. in 2010, an estimated 98.6 billion plastic bags were used in the eu. that is about 198 plastic bags per eu citizen. most of the carrying bags are made of lightweight plastic, which is less likely to be reused than plastic bags made of stronger material. austria uses 51 plastic bags per person per year, well below the eu average. so i very much welcome the approach of the european commission, which is to let the eu countries decide for themselves how to reduce the consumption of plastic bags. each country has its own circumstances and should decide for itself whether taxes, levies or bans are the best way to go!
in writing. - the protection of human life is a priority for all eu action. the most important thing, therefore, especially in reports like this, is to ensure that human rights are respected and that human lives are not endangered in any way. the trafficking and smuggling of human beings in the mediterranean has increased dramatically in recent years, and this geographical area needs to be better monitored. this is not primarily about surveillance; the protection of human life is the highest priority.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report which establishes new funding rules for political parties and european political foundations. the aim of the report is to propose a new financing method which is done according to parliamentʼs resolution ‘which considers that ... the financing of european political parties and european political foundations should be improvedʼ. political parties should be financed through a new instrument, through ‘contributionsʼ, and european political foundations should still be financed through an operating grant as in the past. in my opinion this report is a very technical and organisational detail and instrument in the actual budgetary system of the european institutions.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report as it represents a set of rules established during trilogues and negotiations between the european institutions (parliament, the commission and the council) with regard to the financial regulation. in our opinion this needed a couple of amendments in order to make the ‘carry-overʼ rules more efficient and relevant to the new financing programmes and proposals (new mff programming). in adopting this report the financial regulation will be amended in accordance with the outcome of the last negotiations and adapted to the new multiannual financial framework and financing programmes proposed (and adopted) by the commission and parliament.

mr president, the system of own resources of the eu should and must take off the burden of the financial contribution from the member states. the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu), especially article 311, refers to financial autonomy and explicitly specifies that the eu has the possibility to establish new own resources or to abolish existing own resources. in this sense, in the legislative procedure for the adoption of own resources, the council should act unanimously and after consulting the european parliament. it did not happen again, taking into consideration the limited changes proposed by the council, such as: one, changing the ceiling for payment appropriations to 1.23[nbsp ]% of the eu gni; two, changing the ceiling for commitment appropriations to 1.29[nbsp ]% of the eu gni; and three, ignoring the fact that the commission proposal on how to make own resources available – which would have actually decreased the member states’ gni contributions – still needs to be analysed and worked on. taking into consideration the current economic situation across europe, this change is still insignificant for the national budgets of the member states – and, looking further, for the budgets of our citizens. bearing this in mind, and the fact that we need fully to respect the principle of fiscal sovereignty of the member states, i believe we should accept and accelerate the proposal, the high-level group activity and own resources system implementation in order to be able to present concrete and real results to our taxpayers.

the commission has already made a number of proposals. the decision of the european court of justice on 8 april this year is indeed something of a liberating blow for civil rights on this continent, for 500 million citizens. the european court of justice, as my colleague judith sargentini has already said, has ruled against fear and intimidation and in favour of fundamental rights. and for that, he really deserves a big thank you. i want to briefly touch on the history of why and how this stone came into being in the first place. this was in early 2012, when my green austrian national council colleague, our justice spokesman albert steinhauser, together with the working group on data retention decided to bring a case against data retention to the austrian constitutional court. it took a few months, and a total of 11139 signatures were collected - mine was there - and this was the largest constitutional lawsuit of the republic of austria. the austrian constitutional court has also accepted the action based on the matters already discussed today. the commission has also proposed that the court of justice should, in the case of a case of infringement of fundamental rights, give its opinion on the application of the principle of proportionality. and even if there are isolated cases, it is clear that the most effective means have not been used. whether there are any positive effects in these individual cases is not really certain either. these serious intrusions into privacy are disproportionate. i am very glad that the austrian constitutional court then went to the european court of justice and that court supported the concerns of the austrians who submitted these signatures and said: disproportionate and above all inefficient. that is to say, with this judgment it is clear that this data retention and the laws that exist at national level should also be abolished.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the ecj's ruling on data retention is an important piece of case law. the german journalist heribert prantl even said that this would mark a turning point in the protection of fundamental rights in europe. however, the ruling comes at a historic moment in the protection of private data. it's a reminder to all those who believed in the wake of 9/11 that the mass accumulation of data on inventory and the creation of oversized data warehouses inside and outside europe would lead to greater security. the court of justice found that the constant feeling of being watched was a source of insecurity for european citizens. in his opinion, the retention of data constitutes a violation of fundamental rights. it is therefore incompatible with european law. the court held that the directive infringed the principles of necessity, proportionality and proportionality. the judgment proves that the european institutions are working. but at the same time it is a wake-up call that we must take very seriously. to simply go along with the agenda would be fatal. for the european legislator, the judgment means that he must implement it and, in a future directive, ensure that the framework is narrow and must be differentiated on an individual basis. whether data retention is still useful is a valid question. the concerns of the citizens must be taken into account. the european legislator is also called upon to review existing legal bases such as the eprivacy directive, various passenger data agreements or swift for their compliance with fundamental rights, and to do so quickly. the member states must also review their legal position, since they can no longer rely on this european legal basis. in certain cases they will probably have to amend or repeal their laws. in any case, the time for a blanket, undifferentiated, random round-trip storage is over.
member of the commission. - mr president, as i said initially, the commission welcomes this judgment by the court, as it reflects very much the criticisms that we had in our own evaluation a couple of years ago. we are assessing the full implications of the judgment. it takes time and we need to carefully assess all this with our legal experts. however, a few things are clear already. first of all, as you have all said, this declaration on invalidity takes place immediately from the date the directive entered into force. that means that we are back to the situation before the adoption of the data retention directive in 2006 and that is also why the commission has taken the necessary steps to withdraw the case against germany and that is why the fines given to sweden will be paid back. it is also clear from the judgment that member states’ national legislations are not directly concerned by the ruling. each member state has to assess whether there is a need to change national legislation. it will be up to national jurisdictions to decide if the legislation in question fully respects the fundamental rights. there were some questions on the pnr and the tftp agreement. of course we are carefully assessing and reassessing this, but it seems that the agreements provide for enough specific safeguards and are reviewed regularly by a team which includes representatives of the national data protection authorities. we do not see any link between the court ruling and these agreements. but we will probably come back to this. concerning the european pnr directive that the commission has proposed and that we have discussed many times in this plenary, these two issues are not comparable. the proposed eu pnr directive addresses all the issues and concerns raised by the court ruling on the data retention directive because it would strictly regulate the access to data and its subsequent use. it will be limited to trained experts in a passenger information unit. the use of the data will be limited to the combating of serious crime and terrorism and any processing of sensitive data is prohibited. the proposal also includes effective safeguards to ensure protection of the data. we are ready to work with you – with the next parliament – on the proposal for the eu pnr directive. we can assess together whether the strict limitations and safeguards can be further strengthened. there was a recently adopted paper by the eu fundamental rights agency, which provides very useful inspiration. what will happen now? it is too early to say. mr weber, we cannot present anything in a couple of days. this needs very careful assessment. if there were to be a new proposal presented – and i said ‘if’ – that would, of course, take into account the outcome of the court ruling but also the data protection reform that has been debated here so many times. we need to see progress on this. you might recall that we discussed a couple of weeks ago the post-stockholm programme and the paper by the commission ‘an open and secure europe’. we said in that paper that we would review the data retention directive. that was written before the judgment. taking into account the data protection reforms: if there were to be a proposal on a new type of data retention directive, taking into account what the court says, of course that will be dealt with in the normal legislation, certainly with full participation by the european parliament, thus guaranteeing the quality of it. but it is too early to say; i am sure that we will be able to come back to this when we have carefully looked at and analysed all the legal aspects of this.
president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy - mr president, the issues addressed in parliament’s draft resolution are diverse, and very important and wide-ranging. let me comment, on behalf of the vice-president/high representative, catherine ashton, on some elements that could help in fuelling today’s debate. the european union intends to carry on promoting and defending, internally and externally, the very principles on which it was built – respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law. with the adoption, in june 2012, of the eu strategic framework on human rights and democracy, the european union recalled that, throughout the world, women and men demanded to live in liberty, dignity and security, in open and democratic societies underpinned by human rights and the rule of law. the eu committed itself to enhanced efforts to uphold the universality of these values. one of the first outcomes of the 2012 strategy was the adoption of european union guidelines on freedom of religion or belief, to be used in its external policies. these guidelines have been used in delegations and headquarters to better engage with third countries, bilaterally and multilaterally, notably in the fight against all forms of intolerance and discrimination on grounds of religion or belief and with the implementation of the relevant un resolutions in this field. furthermore, in a joint statement of 20 september 2012, the high representative and the representatives of three organisations – the organisation of islamic cooperation, the african union and the arab league – called for peace and tolerance between religions and expressed their common belief in the fundamental importance of religious freedom and tolerance. they also condemned any advocacy of religious hatred. religious beliefs were not to be abused to fuel extremism and confrontation. they also condemned violence and attacks against diplomatic missions around the world. they asked all political leaders, be they religious or secular, to call for dialogue and tolerance. ‘the only answer to the darkness of intolerance and ignorance is the light of mutual respect, tolerance and dialogue.’ i quote from this statement. high representative/vice-president cathy ashton and the external action service, together with the european union special representative, mr[nbsp ]lambrinidis, have taken this forward at all levels and have condemned religious intolerance and discrimination on grounds of religion or belief, wherever it happens. the high representative herself has been particularly vocal in denouncing violence on the basis of religion, such as in the case of the central african republic, where, on 27 march, she strongly condemned the targeted killings of civilians on the basis of religion and ethnicity and expressed her concern about the vulnerability of minorities, who are increasingly victims of retaliation. while stressing the need to fight impunity, she also expressed support for the efforts made by the transitional authorities to promote dialogue and mediation initiatives. the european union has been engaged in initiatives of intercultural and inter-religious dialogue in the spirit of openness, engagement and mutual understanding, including in the framework of unesco, the un alliance of civilisations, the anna lindh foundation and the istanbul process. with the signature of the unesco-eu memorandum of understanding in 2012, a strengthened cooperation was launched. we share common goals, notably to consolidate democracy and human rights, preserve peace and foster sustainable development. this is why the european union clearly promotes stronger multilateral cooperation. eu funding to unesco projects includes, for example, support for training for young syrian refugees in jordan, the expert facility aiming at strengthening governance for culture in 13 countries, the safeguarding of living cultural heritage in egypt, jordan and lebanon and the preservation and restoration of syrian cultural heritage, or of timbuktu’s manuscripts. education and culture are key pillars of the democratic society that we want. education will remain a strong part of the overall eu development framework. education shall promote understanding and respect for human rights, inclusion, cultural diversity, lifelong learning and learning to live together, all of which are essential to the realisation of peace, responsible citizenship and sustainable development. unesco’s role in the global education first initiative remains important. we see culture as an enabler and driver of development. support to culture is clearly support to development. a high-level meeting in new york on 5 may 2014, organised by unesco, will be the venue for further discussions on the important link between culture and development. the eu is also a strong defender of the diversity of cultural expression. we were instrumental in the adoption of the 2005 unesco convention and one of the european union’s main objectives in our relations with third countries is to support cultural policy development and to promote this convention. under the leadership of commissioner vassiliou, and with the active participation of our delegation in beijing, china has become the first pilot case, illustrating the role of culture in people-to-people diplomacy and mutual understanding in the framework of our foreign relations. the secretary general of the external action service, mr pierre vimont, has recently appointed in his office a coordinator on cultural matters, who is working in complementarity with member states also promoting cooperation in this field. the european external action coordinator is active in making contact with a great variety of stakeholders, with a deep engagement in the international cultural scene. the ‘more europe’ initiative, supported by civil society, is also active in bringing together several actors. the european union national institutes for culture association has also been in the frontline. parliament’s resolution rightly stressed the importance of the fight against the death penalty. we have a strong and principled abolitionist policy on that. we firmly believe that no cultural difference or perception could ever contest the fundamental right to life and human dignity. we have publicly condemned – and continue to do so – the use of the death penalty in any circumstances and in any country. we never cease to stress, either in our dialogues with third countries or through public diplomacy, the cruelness and irreversibility of this archaic form of punishment. the eu guidelines on the death penalty clearly instruct us to act whenever and wherever this abominable practice takes place. in the un context, the european union has played a pivotal role in the adoption of the general assembly resolution on the moratorium on the death penalty and will continue this practice in this year’s upcoming general assembly.

in writing. a major reason for the high level of youth unemployment in many member states is the economic and debt crisis in europe, in which companies are more likely to retain or even reduce existing staff than to recruit young people. this is why a sustained crisis management is the most effective measure to combat youth unemployment! euro-area members need to consolidate their budgets in line with the stability and growth pact and implement structural reforms, as this is the only way to achieve sufficient economic growth leading to job creation. in addition, member states should introduce measures to make it more attractive for companies to recruit new staff, especially young people. the following measures are appropriate: - the reduction in the tax burden. - a relief from labor costs. in austria, non-wage labour costs account for 49.1% of total wages. - measures to increase the willingness of enterprises to undertake training, such as the so-called "blum-tausender" which enterprises in austria received for training apprentices. this has led to a sharp increase in youth employment in austria. - the increase in the attractiveness of dual training, a system which in austria and germany is responsible for relatively low youth unemployment compared with other member states. the dual training system is an ideal "best practice" for the countries of europe.

i have to say, madam president, we are discussing a resolution today which calls on all member states to do something they should have done a long time ago, namely to ratify the kampala amendments. why is this so important? this process would further develop international criminal justice, thereby strengthening its reach and its binding nature. the european union has a duty to ensure that the rights of the palestinian people are respected and that the palestinian people are protected. but so far the international criminal court has been unable to develop jurisdiction for crimes of aggression. the rome statute, on which it was based, does not contain a detailed definition of the facts. that is why, so far, members of the military and political leadership cannot be held accountable for instigating an act of aggression that violates the un charter's prohibition of violence. as things stand, these groups cannot be held personally responsible for ordering or providing their territory for such actions as illegal invasions, bombings, blockades of ports or the dispatch of armed gangs. when you hear that, you can clearly remember some of the incidents of the past few weeks. it is only through the kampala amendments, which were adopted after lengthy negotiations, that the crime of aggression is defined. we also know the conditions for how many countries would have to ratify it. it is a pity that only eight eu countries have completed this process. other member states are involved, including my home country, austria. i would like to make one further point: the punishment of crimes is done primarily because it is attributed a deterrent effect. crimes of aggression are crimes of conduct, and aiding and abetting is explicitly excluded. it has often happened that the perpetrators were punished, but those who ordered the crimes went free. the amendments to be ratified will break this unjust debt reversal. they are a clear signal to those responsible to be aware of their responsibility as leaders, because in future crimes of aggression must not go unpunished.

mr president, mr president of the council! i would like to return to the agencies now. the agencies are legally separate from the eu institutions, and are separate legal entities set up to carry out certain tasks under eu law. gerek, the body of european regulators for electronic communications, is one of the decentralised agencies that perform technical, scientific and administrative tasks and support the eu institutions in implementing policy. in this way, they promote the pooling of expertise and know-how in the eu institutions and national authorities, and cooperation between the eu and the governments of the eu countries. the decentralised agencies are set up in the various countries for an indefinite period. we relieved most of the agencies this spring, except for gerek. as has been said today, it was not because there were gross errors here, but because there were a number of small inconsistencies or omissions which took time to clarify. i think it is worth noting that there are inaccuracies in budget monitoring, improvements in the preparation, implementation and documentation of the procurement procedures, lack of information on policy in the case of conflicts of interest, lack of transparency in declarations of financial interests, etc. gerek has of course been given the opportunity to comment on all these allegations. they did, and we got an office report in july, and it shows that most of these allegations have been corrected and there will be improvements in the future. we therefore believe that, following this report, berec should be given a discharge. i must also say today that i would like to thank my colleagues very much for their cooperation with the agencies, but also for the good cooperation with the court of auditors. i believe that this is the way to ensure that the tax money of the european taxpayer is used in a sensible, efficient and productive way.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. over the last few years, more than 40 000 jobs have been lost in the european steel industry. and thousands more will follow, if we can believe the words of the president of the world steel association, mr eder, who said this in a recent interview. mr eder is the ceo of the largest austrian steel company, voestalpine ag. this company has been in the news a lot this year because it's outsourcing its production to the united states. the company cited the high tax and duty burden in austria, the high energy costs, the high environmental requirements and the lack of reform intentions of the federal government as reasons for this outsourcing. the company also criticised the eu's expensive and strict co2 regulations. from 2020 alone, voestalpine ag expects to spend eur 230 million annually on the purchase of emission allowances. this situation is characteristic of the steel industry and of the whole of europe's energy-intensive industry and is leading to a deindustrialisation of europe. the american government, on the contrary, is going to go into massive reindustrialization, incentivizing companies to move in. unfortunately, this is not the case in europe. the degree of reindustrialisation was not agreed. that is why i support this initiative, today's resolution on the european steel industry, and the commission's action plan to re-industrialise europe.

in writing. manufacturing is the backbone of the european economy. the steel industry is in a special position. the sustainable strengthening of the steel sector is essential for a new recovery in europe, including a boost to employment. however, the european steel industry has been under intense competitive pressure and restructuring for many years. i have signed the resolution on the protection of workers and industries in the steel industry in the eu. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. finally, a large number of subcontractors and services are directly linked to the steel sector. this creates jobs in the eu and contributes to a strong european economy. the key is to maintain the quality of jobs. the well-trained workers in the steel industry must be protected accordingly and involved from the outset in restructuring. the rights to information and consultation must therefore be strengthened.

in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution because in the next few years a clean reindustrialisation of europe must be promoted. we need an industry in the european union based on innovation and employment. one of the greatest challenges of the next few years will be to bring new, promising industries to europe. the basis for this is the european steel industry. as a linzer, i myself come from a steel region. steel is synonymous with growth, innovation and employment and has always played an important role in the european economy. a functioning industry is a prerequisite for growth in europe. the outsourcing of industrial jobs abroad leads to the loss of important jobs and increases the risk of a decline in the quality of products. in addition, it is important to reduce cheap imports from countries with low social and environmental standards. this motion for a resolution takes account of the social and environmental components as well as the economic aspects. the resolution is therefore to be welcomed.

in writing. i reject an association agreement with georgia for the same reasons as the one with the republic of moldova. in times of economic difficulties, it is not advisable to pump money from the european union's already tight budget into countries to increase their competitiveness in the european single market without bringing about rapid improvements. georgia, like ukraine, needs long-term assistance, which we cannot afford at this time. the political aspect of rapprochement with georgia must also be taken into account. as the example of moldova shows, an association agreement with georgia can lead to russia imposing massive sanctions against that country. the union would also have to be liable for the economic losses caused by this.
